thread.title: The Week Ahead: Should You Buy Or Sell Based On Election Results?

author: Tom Aspray
title: The Week Ahead: Should You Buy Or Sell Based On Election Results?
text:
Share to facebook Share to twitter Share to linkedin
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, U.S., on Friday, Nov. 2, 2018. SPhotographer: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg
The on-again, off-again trade war with China, along with Apple’s earnings, dominated the stock market last week. During the summer, it seemed like the swings in the trade war sentiment did not affect the markets. Now, however, it seems that the prospects of a trade war are being taken far more seriously.
The Trump administration's comments about $257 billion in new tariffs erased the gains early Monday, which turned into a massive reversal that pushed the major averages lower for the day, despite the strong open. Suggestions by President Trump early Friday that he and the Chinese President were “working on a deal” also gave the market a brief boost early Friday, though later comments from Larry Kudlow supported the view that this was just a pre-election ploy.
TomAspray-ViperReport.com
Even though stocks closed lower on Friday, it was a very good week for the stock market, after four weeks of sharp declines. Despite the weekly gain of 2.42%, the S&P 500 is still just over 7% below its record closing level. The two most beaten-down averages, the small cap Russell 2000 and Dow Jones Transportation Average, had the most impressive gains up 4.32% and 4.02% respectively.
The action last week should have helped convince investors that the recent market decline did not mean that the bull market was over. In Thursday’s “A Survivor’s Guide To Market Corrections” , I examined the current market decline, as well as several similar corrections that have occurred during this bull market. This, I believe, will make investors better able to weather and recover from future market declines.
Friday’s much stronger-than-expected jobs report was another sign that the economy was strong, but still it was a negative for some investors, as it could be a sign that the economy was overheating. It may mean that the Federal Reserve will have to raise rates faster than they have planned.
TomAspray-ViperReport.com
In every market cycle, many investors seem to forget that once rates begin moving higher, it typically takes some time before it becomes a negative for the economy and the stock market. Rates started to raise in 2003 (line a), but the Fed did not move rates higher until the middle of 2004. Rates peaked in 2006, but the stock market did not top until October 2007. while the recession began in early 2008.
The 10-year yield (in pink) started to turn higher in 2016 and has just been rising for two years. This implies that rates could move higher for another year or two without seriously impacting the stock market. The homebuilding stocks topped out in 2006, but the overall market still kept moving higher.
Most of the economic reports last week came in lower than expected, as the Chicago PMI, at 58.4, was below the consensus estimate of 60.0. The ISM Manufacturing Index was 57.7, down 2.1 points from last month, as new orders dropped 4.4 points. On Friday, Factory Orders were stronger than expected, so there were no clear signs last week of a change in the economic trend.
This week, we have the ISM Non-Manufacturing Index and the PMI Services Index on Monday with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey on Tuesday. This measures the difference between the demand for labor and the supply of labor, which has widened sharply in the past few months.
There was considerable technical improvement last week, but there was not enough for me to confirm that the correction is over. Typically after a sharp correction, the stock market needs time before it can recover and move higher.
TomAspray-ViperReport.com
The Spyder Trust (SPY) has dropped below the weekly starc- band for three of the past four weeks. It had a low of $259.85, as it dropped slightly below the weekly support (line a). The decline has so far held above the stronger support at $256.59 that I discussed last weekend .
The rally on Friday came close to the 50% retracement resistance at $276.53 before it reversed. The declining 20-week EMA at $278.55 represents further resistance. The weekly S&P 500 A/D line has turned up, but is still below its flat WMA. Therefore, a positive close and good A/D numbers are needed this week to indicate that the correction is really over.
The advance/decline analysis looks the most positive on the Dow Industrials, so the SPDR Dow Industrials (DIA) looks to have the best potential, followed by the SPY. The iShares Russell (IWM) was up 6.1% from Monday’s low, but despite the impressive rally, the weekly Russell 2000 A/D line is still well below its WMA.
Of course, the focus last week was on Amazon.com (AMZN) and Apple Inc. (AAPL). AMZN had a weekly low of $1476, but then closed at $1665, up 1.4% for the week. It is still holding well above the April lows at $1352. The weekly On-Balance Volume (OBV) and relative performance (RS) have turned upward, but are still negative overall. However, given the extent of this decline, it seems like the $1476 lows will hold.
Personally, I was not surprised that the market did not like Apple’s report. The stock was sold heavily in after-hours trading and in Friday’s session, where AAPL lost 6.6%. There are no signs yet from the technical studies that the decline in AAPL is over, with next good support in the $196-$200 area.
TomAspray-ViperReport.com
Since AMZN and AAPL make up over 22% of the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), it is also not surprising that QQQ has been under pressure. It did gain 1.65% last week, and formed a doji with a high of $172.55 and a low of $160.09. The high was just below the 50% retracement resistance at $173.79, with the 61.8% resistance at $177.04. The weekly Nasdaq 100 A/D line has turned up, but requires a strong close this week to turn positive. It is well above the long term support (line a). The daily A/D line does not yet show a completed bottom formation.
Some on Wall Street believe that a Republican victory in the election will be positive for the market, and that stocks will be in trouble if the Democrats win enough to shift control of Congress. Therefore there is likely to be a knee-jerk reaction in either case. My view, based on the technical action, is to be buying on a pullback towards last week’s lows no matter who wins.
